subject: religious-studies
title: Cosmological Arguments
welcome_lead: Trace the argument from contingency from Aristotle's Unmoved Mover through Aquinas's Five Ways to the contemporary Kalam.
meta_desc: A-Level Religious Studies adventure on cosmological arguments: Aquinas's first three ways, Leibniz on sufficient reason, and the Kalam.
final_note: You have followed cosmological reasoning from contingency through sufficient reason to Big Bang cosmology.

walkthroughs.body_html: In Summa Theologiae I, Q.2, a.3, Aquinas presents the Five Ways. The First Way moves from motion to an Unmoved Mover. The Second Way from efficient causation to a First Cause. The Third Way from contingency to a Necessary Being. Each rejects an actual infinite regress of essentially ordered causes and arrives at what 'all men call God'.

Leibniz, in The Principles of Nature and Grace (1714), asks 'why is there something rather than nothing?' Even an eternal series of contingent beings would not explain itself. The reason must lie in a substance whose existence is necessary in itself, namely God. Hume and Russell objected that the universe might simply be a brute fact.

William Lane Craig revived the Kalam: (1) whatever begins to exist has a cause; (2) the universe began to exist; (3) therefore the universe has a cause. Premise (2) appeals to Big Bang cosmology and the philosophical impossibility of a completed actual infinite. Critics question whether causation applies before time existed, and whether quantum vacuum fluctuations count as 'beginning without a cause'.

It is the question of whether the devil really exists.

Five distinct arguments for God's existence: from motion, causation, contingency, gradation of being, and final causes/teleology — collectively forming Aquinas's natural theology, not a single argument.
Aquinas's Five Ways are five steps of one cosmological argument.
Aquinas's Five Ways are five Christian sacraments.

mcqs.q: What does the cosmological argument try to prove?
options: Aquinas's Five Ways are five Christian sacraments.
The cosmological argument proves who created life on Earth.
The cosmological argument proves the Big Bang happened.
That the existence of the universe requires a first cause or necessary being — usually identified with God — to explain why anything exists at all.

mcqs.q: What is the problem of evil?
options: It is the question of whether the devil really exists.
It is the question of whether evil people will go to hell.
The cosmological argument proves the Big Bang happened.
If God is all-loving, all-knowing and all-powerful, why does evil and suffering exist? Logically, all four cannot be true together without explanation.

mcqs.q: How many 'ways' does Aquinas present in ST I Q.2 a.3?
Craig's defence of the Kalam argument's second premise — the universe began to exist — appeals to:
options: the impossibility of an actual infinite series of past events, supported by Big Bang cosmology
the principle that existence is a perfection
the testimony of religious experience

mcqs.q: Aquinas's Second Way denies that anything can be the efficient cause of itself because:
options: it would have to exist prior to itself, which is impossible
efficient causes are only found in machines
everything is its own cause in nature
efficient causes are identical to final causes

mcqs.q: Against Copleston's demand for a total explanation, Russell maintained that:
options: explaining each member of a series is enough — the whole series needs no further explanation
the universe is its own sufficient reason
God is the explanation of the universe
explanation is impossible in science

mcqs.q: Hume's empiricist critique of the cosmological argument includes the claim that:
options: the idea of a logically necessary being is incoherent, since anything conceivable as existing is conceivable as not existing
causation is directly observed as a necessary connection
the universe cannot be conceived at all
a priori reasoning is the only path to knowledge of causes
